title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 6: Q & A During the "Chamber-to-Chamber" Dialogues
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- a compiled question-and-answer record of the Supreme Court's 'Chamber-to-Chamber' Dialogues with the business community, prefaced by CJP's answer to the standing complaint that judges 'tended to dampen business activity by deciding economic issues, over which they allegedly have no expertise.'

His framing distinction: courts do not decide strictly economic questions like deregulation, devaluation, oil taxes, a new airport or reclamation, which belong to policymakers -- but when officials violate the Constitution or gravely abuse their discretion the judiciary is duty-bound to step in, so that 'the judiciary settles and decides issues that are constitutional and legal, not economic or business.'

The Dialogues as an information-gap project -- held in eleven key areas with a grant from The Asia Foundation and with special sessions for ECOP, the LMCP and the Bangko Sentral's Investor Services Unit -- designed to demystify the judiciary, publicize its reforms, hear business concerns and exchange views.

The substance of the answers: the state of judicial vacancies and pay, the appointment process, delay and its remedies, courthouse infrastructure, discipline of lawyers and judges, why mega-contracts were nullified, and how entrepreneurs can avoid that business risk.
sub_topics: He states the criticism plainly -- business leaders have for years accused the judiciary of interfering in the economic life of the country -- then concedes that questions of deregulation, privatization, globalization, devaluation, oil taxes, a new international airport or Manila Bay reclamation belong to the political departments.

He draws the line: when officials violate the Constitution or the law or gravely abuse their discretion, the judiciary upon proper petition is duty-bound to step in; judicial decisions may affect the economy, but the courts merely discharge their duty to protect public interest by championing the rule of law.

He describes the project's four stated aims and its reach -- the National Capital Region, Davao, Cebu, Laguna, Zamboanga, Baguio, Iloilo, Cagayan de Oro, Pampanga, Subic and Palawan -- with answers given in simple, non-legal language by a panel including Justices Quisumbing, Carpio and Azcuna and court administrators Perez, Dujua and Khan.

Vacancies: as of December 2003, 710 of 2,214 judicial positions, or 32.07 percent, were vacant, mainly because there are few qualified applicants and the Constitution requires the JBC to submit at least three nominees for every vacancy.

Compensation: judges are paid less than new lawyers in Makati firms -- about P25,000 to P30,000 against about P50,000 a month -- so a new law doubled judicial pay in 25 percent increments over four years while the Court asks Congress for exemption from the Salary Standardization Law.

Appointments: the Court has no direct power over them, since the JBC nominates and the President appoints, and aspiring judges must first pass PhilJA's mandatory pre-judicature program, described as the 'pre-cleansing process' in nomination.

Delay: the Constitution allows three months for lower courts, twelve for the Court of Appeals and twenty-four for the Supreme Court, counted from the last pleading; dockets are to be decongested through ADR, a new Office of Alternative Dispute Resolution signed into law on April 2, 2004, and a piloted two-judge mediator-then-trial system in San Fernando and Bacolod.

ADR explained: mediation, arbitration and conciliation are distinguished, with mediation the most widely used; Chief Justice Davide pushed it through PhilJA from 2001, and after 400 mediators were trained a ten-day pilot produced an 81 percent settlement rate and saved the government about P54 million, while the DOJ's own experiment with 60 trained prosecutors reached 93 percent.

Monitoring and technology: a computer-assisted Case-Flow Management system piloted in Pasay City transmits case developments electronically to the Office of the Court Administrator, alongside real-time transcription machines and the Computer-Aided Legal Research electronic library.

Infrastructure: the Committee on Halls of Justice oversees courtroom construction but lacks funding, leaving courts dependent on local governments, though foreign-assisted model courthouses are planned for Angeles City, Lapulapu City and Cagayan de Oro City, and 'mobile courts' on the Guatemalan model are proposed for areas with none.

Discipline: the Court acts on lawyers through the Office of the Bar Confidant and refers complaints to the IBP, accepting its recommendation ninety percent of the time, having disciplined about 58 lawyers in 2003; judges file monthly reports, soon to be automated through CAMIS, and anonymous complaints with verifiable documents prompt discreet OCA investigation.

Contract nullification: only about 2 percent of contracts brought for nullification are voided, and the mega-contracts were struck down on the principle of 'leveling the playing field' -- Comelec's automation award violated the bidding law and Comelec's own rules, the Piatco contract awarded was not the one implemented, and Amari reiterated that private entities could not own foreshore land.

Advice to entrepreneurs: consult a good lawyer before entering a contract rather than after trouble; avoid shortcuts because the law will be upheld regardless of consequences; and do not bribe judges or believe lawyers who say bribery is necessary, since the corrupt judges dismissed by the Court are very few compared with the many ethical ones.

Jurisdictional answers: the Court has administrative supervision over all judges including those in the ARMM; labor cases begin with the NLRC and reach the Court only through the Court of Appeals; and DARAB decisions travel to the Office of the President, the Court of Appeals and then the Court.

Jails and special courts: the judiciary has no jurisdiction over jail management, though the IBP runs the 'Balik Laya' decongestion project in Manila and Pasay; tribal communities are served through IPRA training for judges under the RAJCA project with PhilJA and USAID; and special commercial courts already exist by the November 21, 2000 Resolution, with the business community asked to help police bouncing-check cases.

The epilogue calls the project a small detail in an extensive reform program whose importance lies in the challenges the business sector pressed on the judiciary, with the long-term goal of 'a justice system that is fair and efficient as well as predictable and stable.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's compilation of the questions and answers from the Supreme Court's 'Chamber-to-Chamber' Dialogues with the business community, prefaced by his own framing essay. He acknowledged that business leaders had long accused judges of dampening business by deciding economic issues over which they had no expertise, and conceded that deregulation, privatization, globalization, devaluation, oil taxation and whether to build an airport or reclaim Manila Bay were questions for policymakers. But when officials violated the Constitution or gravely abused their discretion, he wrote, the judiciary was duty-bound to step in; judicial decisions might affect the economy, yet the courts decided constitutional and legal rather than economic questions and merely championed the rule of law. The Dialogues, assisted by a grant from The Asia Foundation, were held in eleven key areas and in special sessions for ECOP, the LMCP and the Bangko Sentral's Investor Services Unit, with answers given in non-legal language by a panel of justices and court administrators. The compiled answers covered the 710 vacancies among 2,214 judicial positions as of December 2003 and their causes in low pay and the three-nominee rule; the JBC-and-President appointment process and PhilJA's pre-judicature program; constitutional periods for deciding cases and remedies for delay through alternative dispute resolution, a new ADR office, and a piloted two-judge system; mediation's 81 percent pilot success rate and the DOJ's 93 percent; computerized case-flow management, transcription and legal research; courthouse funding, model courthouses and proposed mobile courts; discipline of lawyers through the IBP and of judges through monthly reports and OCA investigation; and jurisdictional questions on the ARMM, labor cases, DARAB appeals, jails, tribal justice and commercial courts. On contracts he reported that only about 2 percent are voided, that the mega-contracts fell on the principle of leveling the playing field, and that entrepreneurs should consult counsel early, avoid shortcuts and never bribe judges.
